<margin>Commentary by Su</margin> To not know the Way but strive for academic knowledge means that as one hears and sees more, one fails to unify these experiences. This inevitably leads to becoming burdened. Confucius said, "To hear much, select the good and follow it; to see much and remember it, this is a secondary level of knowledge." If one truly knows the Way, one realizes that falsehood is everywhere. To remove falsehood and restore one's nature is what is meant by "diminishing." When Confucius asked Zigong, "Do you think that I am someone who learns many things and remembers them?" and Zigong replied, "Yes, is it not so?" Confucius answered, "No, I unify it all with one thread." To forget the mind so that it becomes pure and restores its original nature is the true meaning of diminishing. If one does not stop there but also forgets this very mind that is seeking purity, only then is there nothing left, and one acts without losing the state of non-action. People all have desires to possess the world and control the principles of affairs. Because they create affairs and seek to control them, their intentions are revealed externally, and things react against them. Therefore, it is difficult and impossible to attain. The Sage does not act, so there are no affairs. Since the mind is not projected outward, things are at peace. Although the Sage does not seek to possess the world or its principles, the world and its principles become orderly and peaceful on their own.

<margin>Commentary by Lü</margin> The study of knowledge is for those who have not yet heard the Way. Since they have not heard the Way, they must seek it broadly, thus it is said "increase." The study of the Way is for those who have already heard it. Since they have already heard it, they must act through non-action, thus it is said "diminish." To diminish and diminish again means one cannot avoid the state of having action. One must also diminish the act of diminishing itself, and only then reach the state of true non-action. Non-action is being silent and unmoving. Doing nothing but leaving nothing undone refers to the state where, upon being stimulated, one permeates all the reasons of the world. To act without action and reach true non-action is the constant. To learn without worry is called spirit. The method of spirit is the Way. Who but the most spiritual can participate in this? Viewed from this perspective, it is clear that one who tries to take the world by constant intervention will find it insufficient to do so.

<margin>Commentary by Huang Maocai</margin> Only when one knows everything can one speak of learning, hence learning seeks to increase day by day. Only when one does nothing can one speak of the Way, hence the Way seeks to diminish day by day. However, "increasing" allows one to progress, while "diminishing" is perhaps difficult to force. Only the extremely wise can suddenly let go and drop everything to reach the ground of non-action, thereby being able to do nothing, yet having their applications be inexhaustible. When applied to the world, they are generous and spacious.

<margin>Commentary by Xizhai</margin> The study of knowledge is used to seek understanding, so it increases day by day. The study of the Way is used to remove falsehood, so it diminishes day by day. If knowledge does not reach its limit, the diminishing will be incomplete. Therefore, "increasing" serves as the foundation for "diminishing." If one diminishes and diminishes again, falsehood is removed and truth is complete, resulting in non-action. Once one reaches non-action, there is no action that is not also non-action. This is no longer a matter of simple increase or decrease. When it comes to the extreme of non-action, even with the multiplicity of the world, all is unified by one thread. If one creates affairs where there are none, it is difficult to find respite. If one is already entangled and conflicted by a single object, how much more so with the complexity of the whole world?

In ancient times, the Son of Heaven had one thousand officials, and the feudal lords had one hundred officials. Those who could make their orders effective across all the states of the <term>Xia</term> <gloss>the central states/China</gloss> using these thousand officials were called Kings. Those who could make their orders effective within their own borders using these hundred officials, even if their state was unstable, were not at risk of being overthrown or destroyed, and were called Rulers. This applies to the descendants of the Sage Kings after they have inherited the world and hold the registers of authority as the ancestral house of the world. However, if they are incompetent and not upright, the common people suffer within, and the feudal lords rebel without. Near at hand, the borders are not unified; far away, the feudal lords do not listen. Their orders are not effective within their borders; at worst, the feudal lords encroach upon, diminish, and attack them. In such a state, even if they have not yet perished, I say they have lost the world. When a Sage King has passed away and the one holding the registers is weak <note>original: 罷, phonetically read as "pi"</note> and unable to hold the world together, the world has no ruler. If among the feudal lords there is one whose virtue is clear and whose prestige has accumulated, so that the people within the seas all desire to have him as their ruler and teacher, and yet a violent state acts with singular excess, how can he not punish it? He must not harm the innocent people, but punish the ruler of the violent state as if punishing a solitary man. If he can do this, he can be called a man who knows how to use the world. To know how to use the world is what it means to be a King. Tang and Wu did not seize the world; they cultivated their Way, practiced their righteousness, shared the common benefits of the world, and eliminated the common harms of the world, and so the world turned toward them. Jie and Zhou did not abandon the world; they acted against the virtues of Yu and Tang, disrupted the distinctions of ritual and righteousness, behaved like beasts, and accumulated their cruelty, thereby losing their subjects.

○ III. Revealing the characteristics of the dependent arising mentioned above: This refers to the phrase regarding the defiled mind.

○ 1. Indication.
The defiled mind has six types.

○ 2. Inquiry.
What are the six?
Within the six, each has two parts: first the obstruction, then the remedy.

○ 3. Explanation.
Although these six defilements are matched in reverse order to the six coarse marks, the first four and the latter three subtle marks [correspond] due to the *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith*, Volume 1. <note>original: 起信論疏卷上</note> This first part corresponds to the three and four in the coarse marks; thus there are only six. Therefore, these names are borrowed to categorize these six.

○ i. The characteristic of attachment and designation.
First, the attachment-corresponding defilement. It is abandoned by those of the Two Vehicles <note>the practitioners of the Shravaka and Pratyekabuddha paths</note> upon their liberation and by those at the stage of faith-correspondence. This corresponds to the third and fourth of the six coarse marks. It is also the meaning of what was increased by the views and afflictions of the consciousness mentioned above, and it is the characteristic of discriminating attachment within the four marks mentioned above. However, since the coarse mind attaches externally to objects and corresponds to the environment, thereby staining one's pure conduct, it is called "defiled." The liberation of the Two Vehicles refers to the ultimate departure from view-afflictions and practice-afflictions at the stage of the Arhat. "Faith-correspondence" refers to those from the Ten Stages of Understanding onward, whose faculties of faith are accomplished and not lost; thus it is called faith-correspondence. The *Treatise on the Ten Stages* <note>original: 地論</note> says that before the stages, they are generally called practitioners of faith. The *Treatise on Non-attachment* <note>original: 無著論</note> says the same. This Bodhisattva

attains the view of emptiness regarding the self; view-afflictions and practice-afflictions cannot manifest, so it is said they are "departed from." This is not to say that latent tendencies <note>original: 隨眠</note> are kept to retain delusion. The *Summary of the Mahayana* <note>original: 攝論</note> says: "If one does not sever the subtle mind, one is not different from an ordinary person; if one does not retain the seeds of delusion, one is not different from those of the Two Vehicles." Furthermore, there are two meanings for retaining delusion: for the sake of oneself and for the sake of others. This is spoken according to the Final Teaching. If one speaks according to the Initial Teaching, it is only from the First Stage upward that one speaks of retaining delusion, as discussed in other treatises. Now, this Bodhisattva does not simply sever the four dwellings and attachment to a self, but also partially severs the dwelling of ignorance. Therefore, this treatise says below: "Those who do not understand the meaning of the One Dharma Realm..." they observe and learn to sever it from the stage of faith-correspondence. Now, it is only to reveal the coarseness of attachment to a self that [the others] are not discussed.

○ ii. The characteristic of continuity.
Second, the continuity-corresponding defilement. It is gradually abandoned by practitioners at the stage of faith-correspondence through the cultivation of skillful means, and it is ultimately departed from at the Stage of Pure Mind.

### Chapter 7: No Acquisition, No Discourse

Subhuti, what do you think? Has the <term>Tathagata</term> <gloss>Thus-Come One/Buddha</gloss> attained <term>anuttara-samyak-sambodhi</term> <gloss>unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment</gloss>? Does the <term>Tathagata</term> have any doctrine to preach?

Subhuti replied: According to my understanding of the meaning of what the Buddha has said, there is no fixed Dharma called <term>anuttara-samyak-sambodhi</term> <gloss>unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment</gloss>, nor is there any fixed Dharma that the <term>Tathagata</term> can preach. Why? Because the teachings spoken by the <term>Tathagata</term> are not to be grasped, cannot be spoken of, are neither phenomena nor non-phenomena. What is the reason for this? All sages and saints are distinguished by their realization of the <term>asamskrta-dharma</term> <gloss>unconditioned, non-phenomenal reality</gloss>.

### Chapter 8: Birth Through the Dharma

Subhuti, what do you think? If a person were to fill the three-thousand-fold world system with the seven treasures and give them as alms, would the merit and virtue obtained by this person be great?

Subhuti replied: Very great, World-Honored One. Why? Because this merit and virtue is not the intrinsic nature of merit and virtue, and that is why the <term>Tathagata</term> speaks of it as great merit and virtue.
